Q: why cannot UTF-8 encoding of unicode code points fit in 3 bytes A:

There are several things to consider here.

Firstly UTF-8 was designed before the dispute between the Unicode and ISO over 16-bit vs 32-bit characters was resolved. As a result the original UTF-8 was designed to support the full 32-bit range potentially used by ISO.

Secondly variable width encodings by their very nature will often end up with a longer maximum length than a fixed-width encoding would. Every time you assign a short sequence to something, you cut into the number of available longer sequences.

Thirdly, encoding size is not the only thing in play in encoding design, there are some other important factors.

  • How easy is the encoding to encode and decode?
  • How well does the encoding recover from errors? if a byte is lost or corrupted how much of the encoded text is lost?
  • Is the encoding safe to search? Specifially this translates to "does a shorter encoding ever appear as a sub-sequence of a longer encoding"?

Q: How can I create a toolbar on pure WINAPI without icons? A:

Three more changes to make it work:

  1. Call this at some point before sending TB_ADDBUTTONS:

    SendMessage(hToolbar, TB_BUTTONSTRUCTSIZE, (WPARAM)sizeof(TBBUTTON), 0);

TB_ADDBUTTONS fails without it.

With this added, you would see two clickable buttons, but they look ugly: there's an empty space for the icon, and the text is cut off.

  1. Add BTNS_AUTOSIZE button style:

    tb.fsStyle = BTNS_BUTTON | BTNS_SHOWTEXT | BTNS_AUTOSIZE;

Now it looks decent - the button fits the text, and the empty space for the icon is gone.

  1. (Optional) Add TBSTYLE_FLAT style in CreateWindow, next to TBSTYLE_LIST. The toolbar looks prettier, more modern this way. This is purely cosmetic.

Q: Matching consecutive duplicate characters in a string in Google Sheets A:

Split the string into characters, go through them individually, and check each against the previous character while building the result string with reduce(), like this:

=reduce(, regexextract(A2, rept("(.)", len(A2))), lambda(a, c,
  a & left(c, right(a) <> c)
))

If you need to work with multi-byte characters, separate the string into characters with split(), remove duplicates with filter(), and combine with join():

=let(
  a, A2,
  s, if(isnumber(a), "→", rept(0, lenb(a) + 1)),
  q, rept(12, lenb(a)),
  t, regexreplace(to_text(a), "'+", q),
  v, arrayformula(to_text(split(regexreplace(t, "(.)", "$1" & s), s,))),
  substitute(join(, ifna(filter(hstack(v,), hstack(v,) <> hstack(,v)))), q, "'")
)

This formula will correctly handle dates, formatted numbers and single quotes ' that often cause trouble with split().

See reduce(), regexextract(), regexreplace(), let(), lenb(), rept(), split(), join(), filter() and hstack().

Q: Last page of a HorizontalPager is particularly sticky A:

This is almost certainly not a Pager bug.

Something on your last page is consuming part of the horizontal drag gesture. Because of that, the pager receives less distance/velocity, so you have to flick harder to go back. When you start the swipe at the far right edge, you’re likely hitting an area that isn’t covered by that gesture-handling composable, so the pager gets the full gesture and it feels normal.

This also explains why it’s more noticeable on some devices like what you have. Different touch slop and gesture sensitivity make partial gesture consumption feel worse.

What you can do is temporarily replace the last page content with a simple Box(fillMaxSize()). If the issue disappears, it’s definitely a gesture conflict inside that page, if not then the problem is not a gesture conflict inside the page but instead related to overscroll effects, snap or fling thresholds, system gesture edge handling, or a version-specific bug in the pager implementation.

Q: pg-promise spy on query functions A:

In case anyone else comes across this in googling, this worked for me:

jest.spyOn(db, 'one').mockResolvedValue(() => jest.fn())
jest.spyOn(db, 'any').mockResolvedValue(() => jest.fn())

Then after that, if you want to specify a value in a test, you can do this kind of thing:

db.any.mockResolvedValueOnce({dataObject})

db.one.mockRejectedValue(new Error({message: 'Not Found', status: 404})

Q: how can you tell if a replace operator was successful A:

  • Indeed, -replace, the regular-expression-based string replacement operator, does not indicate whether an actual replacement was performed; instead, it always returns a string: either the input string as-is, if no replacement took place, or a modified copy.

  • If no replacements are performed, the very same string instance as the input string is returned, which you can take advantage of for a quick test, whose performance is independent of the size of the input string. That is, you can use [object]::ReferenceEquals() to compare the input string to the -replace return value.

For example:

$100mb_str = 'x' * 50mb

$potentiallyModified_str = $100mb_str -replace 'nomatch', 'y'

# Determine if actual replacements took place.
"Were replacements made?"
-not [object]::ReferenceEquals($100mb_str, $potentiallyModified_str)
